question.text: A trader simultaneously buys and sells the same quantity of a derivative contract at the same price through different brokers to create an illusion of trading activity. This is an example of:

answer.text: Wash trade/synchronized trading, which is prohibited under PFUTP regulations
A spread order placed through different brokers

explanation.text: The Logic: Simultaneously buying and selling the same derivative contract in the same quantity at the same price - with no real change in beneficial ownership, position or risk - is the hallmark of a wash trade or synchronized trade. The activity produces only artificial volume and price impressions in the market, misleading other participants. Such trades are treated as fraudulent and unfair trade practices under SEBI's PFUTP framework. The Trap: A legitimate hedge involves offsetting risk between two genuinely different exposures (cash vs futures, different expiries, etc.), arbitrage relies on actual price differentials between markets, and a spread is an intentional pairing of related positions for an economic view - none of which describe identical-price round-tripping with no change in position. Note: The wash trade / synchronized trade scenario is not explicitly covered in the cited pages of the NISM-Series-VIII Equity Derivatives workbook, which on the pages checked discusses legitimate hedging, spread and arbitrage concepts plus broad unfair-practice powers. The framing above is general SEBI PFUTP / market-abuse regulatory knowledge.
